concepts.name: Category and function
concepts.orientation: Every expression can be described twice: by its category (what kind of expression it is, such as noun or NP) and by its function (the role it plays in a larger expression, such as subject or head). The two vary independently.
concepts.note: Traditional terms such as 'adjective clause' or 'noun clause' mix the two dimensions, naming a clause after the function of a word class. The analysis here keeps them apart: a clause can function as subject, complement or modifier, and the label for its category stays Clause.

concepts.name: Constituent structure
concepts.orientation: Sentences are not flat strings of words. Words group into constituents, which group into larger constituents, and the same words can sometimes be grouped in two ways.
concepts.note: The trees in this explorer label every node with its function and category, in the order Function: Category, in the style of the book's trees. Substitution (by a pronoun), movement (fronting) and coordination are ordinary tests for constituents.

concepts.name: Heads and dependents
concepts.orientation: Most constituents have a head, the element that determines what kind of phrase it is, and dependents that attach to it: complements, modifiers and (in the NP) a determiner.
concepts.note: In clause structure the predicate is the head of the clause and the predicator is the head of the VP. Coordinations are not headed: the coordinates are of equal status.

concepts.name: Words and lexemes
concepts.orientation: Takes, took and taken are three different words but forms of one lexeme, take. Inflection produces word forms of a lexeme; lexical word-formation creates new lexemes.
concepts.note: Lexemes are often written in small capitals or italics to distinguish them from their forms; this explorer names the lexeme in the form field, e.g. 'preterite of the lexeme take'.

concepts.name: Sentence and clause
concepts.orientation: A sentence is the largest unit of syntax; a clause is a construction centrally consisting of a subject and a predicate. A sentence may be one clause, contain clauses inside clauses, or be a coordination of clauses.
concepts.note: Traditional 'simple, compound and complex sentence' classifications are not used: the analysis describes which clauses there are and how they combine.

concepts.name: Canonical and non-canonical clauses
concepts.orientation: Canonical clauses are the most elementary kind: main, declarative, positive, active and in basic order. Others, such as subordinate, interrogative, passive or extraposed clauses, are described by how they differ from canonical ones.
concepts.note: Non-canonical does not mean unusual or less correct; it means 'described relative to the canonical construction'.

concepts.name: Verb inflection
concepts.orientation: Verbs have six inflectional forms: preterite (took), 3rd singular present (takes), plain present (take), plain form (take), gerund-participle (taking) and past participle (taken).
concepts.note: The preterite and the two present tense forms are primary forms; the other three are secondary. Traditional grammar's separate 'gerund' and 'present participle' are one form here, the gerund-participle.

concepts.name: The gerund-participle
concepts.orientation: Verbs in -ing are one inflectional form, the gerund-participle, whether they follow progressive be or head a subject clause. Separately, some -ing words are nouns.
concepts.note: The traditional distinction between gerunds (noun-like) and present participles (adjective-like) is not drawn for verbs: no verb shows a form difference between the two uses, and the noun-like and adjective-like properties belong to the clause the verb heads, not to the verb.

concepts.name: Finiteness
concepts.orientation: Finiteness is treated as a property of clauses. Clauses with a tensed verb are finite; so are imperative and subjunctive clauses, although their verb is the untensed plain form.
concepts.note: Because tense marking is so reduced in English, a definition of finiteness by verb inflection alone would misclassify imperatives and subjunctives, whose plain-form verbs are identical to infinitives.

concepts.name: Auxiliary verbs
concepts.orientation: Auxiliaries such as be, have, do and the modals are verbs with special syntax (inversion, negation with not, emphatic polarity). In the analysis followed here they head the VP and take a non-finite clause as complement.
concepts.note: Main-clause interrogatives such as Has Kim left? place the auxiliary before the subject (subject–auxiliary inversion). This version does not draw trees for inverted clauses; see the review notes.

concepts.name: Subject, predicate and predicator
concepts.orientation: A canonical clause consists of a subject and a predicate. The predicate is a VP whose head, the verb, is the predicator; complements and adjuncts are its dependents.
concepts.note: Predicate (a function of the VP in the clause) and predicator (the function of the verb in the VP) are deliberately distinct terms.

concepts.name: Complements vs adjuncts
concepts.orientation: Complements are licensed by a particular head (put needs a location; rely needs on). Adjuncts are not selected and can be added more freely. The same phrase may be either, depending on the head.
concepts.note: Obligatoriness is the clearest sign but not the definition: objects of eat are complements even though eat can be used without one. Licensing by the head is the central criterion.

concepts.name: The subject
concepts.orientation: The subject is identified syntactically: in canonical clauses it precedes the verb, the verb agrees with it, and it inverts with an auxiliary in questions. It is often, but not always, the agent.
concepts.note: Agreement is with the head of the subject NP, which is why the box under the stairs takes is.

concepts.name: Semantic roles and subject
concepts.orientation: Agent, patient, instrument and recipient are semantic roles. Subject and object are syntactic functions. The two are related, but a subject need not be an agent, and an agent need not be a subject.
concepts.note: The 'logical subject' of traditional accounts of the passive corresponds here to the agent role expressed in the by-phrase; it is not a subject.

concepts.name: Objects
concepts.orientation: An object is an NP complement in the VP, typically after the verb, that can usually become the subject of a passive. Content clauses after verbs like know are complements, not objects.
concepts.note: In a monotransitive clause there is just one object, which corresponds to the direct object of a ditransitive.

concepts.name: Ditransitive clauses and indirect objects
concepts.orientation: Ditransitive clauses have two objects: the indirect object (typically recipient) and then the direct object. A to-PP expressing the recipient is not an indirect object.
concepts.note: Some grammars call to Pat in gave a book to Pat an indirect object. Here indirect objects are NPs by definition; the to-phrase is a PP complement.

concepts.name: Predicative complements
concepts.orientation: A predicative complement describes or identifies the subject (Kim became a teacher) or the object (made Pat angry). It may be an AdjP, NP or PP, and it is not an object.
concepts.note: Traditional 'subject complement' and 'object complement' correspond to subjective and objective predicative complements.

concepts.name: Ascriptive and specifying be
concepts.orientation: Be has two main uses with a predicative complement: ascribing a property (Kim is a doctor) and specifying a value (The winner was Kim).
concepts.note: Specifying clauses are generally reversible (Kim was the winner), with the NPs exchanging functions; ascriptive clauses are not.

concepts.name: Prepositional verbs
concepts.orientation: Some verbs select a PP headed by a particular preposition (rely on, look at). The NP is the complement of the preposition, not an object of the verb.
concepts.note: Prepositional passives (The map was looked at) show that the verb–preposition combination behaves as a unit in some respects while the PP remains a constituent in others.

concepts.name: The verb–particle–object construction
concepts.orientation: In looked up the word, up is a particle: a one-word PP complement that can come before or after the object. It is not the head of a PP containing the object.
concepts.note: Particles are intransitive prepositions. Their mobility around the object (and obligatory placement after a pronoun object: looked it up) distinguishes them from prepositions heading a PP.

concepts.name: Nouns and pronouns
concepts.orientation: Nouns head noun phrases. Proper nouns and pronouns are subclasses of noun: she and Kim head NPs just as dog does.
concepts.note: Treating pronouns as nouns reflects their syntax: they head NPs with the same functions (subject, object, complement of a preposition). Their special features, such as case and limited dependents, define the subclass.

concepts.name: Noun phrase structure
concepts.orientation: An NP may contain a determiner and a head nominal; the nominal contains the head noun with its modifiers and complements.
concepts.note: The nominal (Nom) is the unit between NP and noun. The trees show a Nom node when the head noun has modifiers or complements; when the NP has only a determiner and noun, or just a noun, no separate Nom is drawn.

concepts.name: Determiner and determinative
concepts.orientation: Determiner is a function in the NP; determinative is a category of words (the, a, some, every, enough, three). Determinatives are often determiners, but each can occur in the other's absence.
concepts.note: Many grammars use 'determiner' for both the word class and the function. Separate terms make it possible to say that enough is a determinative functioning as modifier in big enough, and that Kim's is an NP functioning as determiner.

concepts.name: Determinatives
concepts.orientation: Determinatives are a closed category including the articles, demonstratives, numerals and quantifying words. Several can also modify adjectives and adverbs.
concepts.note: A one-word determiner is drawn as a bare determinative (Det: D). Determinatives in other functions are drawn as a determinative phrase (DP), since they can take their own dependents (almost all, very much).

concepts.name: Genitives as determiners
concepts.orientation: A genitive NP such as Kim's or my can fill the determiner function. It makes the NP definite, like the, and is called a subject-determiner.
concepts.note: Possessive my, your and their are genitive forms of pronouns heading NPs that function as determiners; they are not adjectives.

concepts.name: Fused heads
concepts.orientation: Sometimes one word does two jobs in the NP: most in most stayed is both determiner and head (fused determiner-head); blue in the blue is both modifier and head (fused modifier-head).
concepts.note: Fused heads are discussed in Chapter 5; the exact section is not cited here because it falls outside the verified contents pages. The analysis avoids positing a silent noun: the determinative or adjective itself is head.

concepts.name: Adjectives
concepts.orientation: Adjectives are identified by function and form: they modify nouns attributively, serve as predicative complements, are often gradable and take adverbs like very.
concepts.note: Attributive modification and predicative complement are both functions of adjective phrases; a one-word AdjP is still a phrase.

concepts.name: Attributive, predicative and postpositive
concepts.orientation: Most adjectives work both before a noun (attributive) and after be (predicative). Some are attributive-only (main), some never attributive (afraid), and a few follow the noun (members present).
concepts.note: These restrictions belong to individual adjectives (lexemes), not to the category as a whole.

concepts.name: Adjective phrases
concepts.orientation: An AdjP has an adjective head with optional modifiers (very, much) and complements (of chocolate, to help).
concepts.note: Complements of adjectives are typically PPs or clauses; adjectives do not take NP objects (*fond chocolate).

concepts.name: Adverbs and adverb phrases
concepts.orientation: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs, but not nouns. The category is narrower here than in traditional grammar: many traditional 'adverbs' are prepositions.
concepts.note: Adverb names a category; adjunct names a function. Many adjuncts are not adverbs (on Monday is a PP), and adverbs can be modifiers within AdjPs and AdvPs.

concepts.name: Prepositions
concepts.orientation: Prepositions head PPs and, in the analysis followed here, may take an NP, a clause or no complement at all. Before, after and because are prepositions throughout.
concepts.note: Treating before in before the meeting ended as a preposition follows the same logic as for verbs, which keep their category whether their complement is an NP or a clause.

concepts.name: Preposition phrases
concepts.orientation: A PP has a preposition head and usually a complement. PPs serve as complements, adjuncts, predicative complements and modifiers in NPs.
concepts.note: When the complement of a preposition is relativised or questioned, the preposition can be left stranded at the end (the person Kim talked to).

concepts.name: Intransitive prepositions
concepts.orientation: Words such as outside, before and up, used without a complement, are prepositions that happen to be intransitive, not adverbs.
concepts.note: The argument parallels verbs: eat with and without an object is one verb; outside with and without an NP is one preposition.

concepts.name: Adjuncts
concepts.orientation: Adjuncts add information about manner, means, instrument, time, place, frequency, reason and more. They may be AdvPs, PPs, NPs or clauses, and can occur at the front, middle or end.
concepts.note: Adjunct is used for modifiers in clause structure. In these trees adjuncts after the verb are dependents within the VP, and front adjuncts are dependents of the clause.

concepts.name: Clause type
concepts.orientation: Clause type is a grammatical system: declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative and imperative clauses differ in form.
concepts.note: Main-clause interrogatives such as Was the shop open? involve subject–auxiliary inversion. This version shows interrogatives through subordinate clauses only and does not draw inverted trees; see the review notes.

concepts.name: Clause type and illocutionary force
concepts.orientation: Clause type is form; illocutionary force (statement, question, directive) is what a speaker does with it. A declarative can be a request, and an imperative can be a wish.
concepts.note: Keeping the two apart explains why 'question' and 'interrogative' are not synonyms.

concepts.name: Subordinators
concepts.orientation: Subordinators (that, whether, interrogative if, for, and infinitival to) mark a clause as subordinate. They are markers, not heads, and they are a much smaller class than traditional 'subordinating conjunctions'.
concepts.note: That in relative clauses is treated as the same subordinator as in content clauses, not as a relative pronoun.

concepts.name: Declarative content clauses
concepts.orientation: Content clauses are the default kind of subordinate finite clause. Declarative ones, often introduced by that, serve as complements of verbs, nouns, adjectives and prepositions, and as subjects.
concepts.note: The traditional label 'noun clause' reflects their functions, not their category: they are clauses, and they are not limited to NP-like positions.

concepts.name: Interrogative content clauses
concepts.orientation: Subordinate interrogatives express questions: closed ones are marked by whether or if; open ones begin with an interrogative phrase in prenucleus position.
concepts.note: Subordinate interrogatives in standard English do not invert: Kim asked whether the shop was open, not ...was the shop open.

concepts.name: Relative clauses
concepts.orientation: A relative clause contains a gap linked to an antecedent. Wh relatives have a relative word (who, which); that relatives use the subordinator that; bare relatives have neither.
concepts.note: Trees mark the relativised position with a gap (__). In wh relatives the gap is linked to the relative phrase in prenucleus position; in that and bare relatives it is understood via the antecedent.

concepts.name: Integrated and supplementary relatives
concepts.orientation: Integrated relatives are part of the NP and usually help identify the referent. Supplementary relatives add separate information, are set off prosodically and by punctuation, and are supplements.
concepts.note: The terms integrated and supplementary describe the syntactic and prosodic relation, avoiding the claim that every integrated relative restricts reference.

concepts.name: Fused relatives
concepts.orientation: In Kim ate what Pat cooked, what Pat cooked is an NP in which what is both head of the NP and the relative phrase of the clause: a fused relative.
concepts.note: Fused relatives are phrases, not clauses: they behave as NPs (as object of ate here). The tree marks the fused element as Head+Prenucleus.

concepts.name: Non-finite clauses
concepts.orientation: Non-finite clauses are headed by a plain form (infinitival), gerund-participle or past participle, and usually lack a subject of their own.
concepts.note: Traditional 'infinitive phrase' and 'participle phrase' are treated as clauses: they have a predicate and can have a subject (for Kim to win).

concepts.name: To-infinitivals
concepts.orientation: In to-infinitivals, to is a subordinator marking the VP, not a preposition. A subject, when present, is introduced by the subordinator for.
concepts.note: Because to is a marker on the VP, an adverb between to and the verb (to quickly leave) is not 'splitting' a word.

concepts.name: The catenative construction
concepts.orientation: Catenative verbs take non-finite clause complements and can form chains (wants to try to leave). In the complex construction an NP intervenes (made Kim laugh).
concepts.note: Auxiliaries are analysed as catenative verbs too, taking a non-finite complement: has in has taken is the predicator.

concepts.name: Gerund-participial clauses
concepts.orientation: A gerund-participial clause is headed by an -ing verb and can be subject, complement or adjunct. It is a clause, not an NP, even when it is a subject.
concepts.note: Contrast with nouns in -ing (the singing): only nouns take determiners and adjectives.

concepts.name: Coordination
concepts.orientation: A coordination joins coordinates of equal status. The coordinator (and, or, but) is a marker on the coordinate it introduces. Coordinates share a function, not necessarily a category.
concepts.note: Treating and as part of the second coordinate explains why and Pat can stand alone (Kim arrived, and Pat) while Kim and cannot.

concepts.name: Supplementation
concepts.orientation: Supplements are loosely attached expressions anchored to a host: appositive NPs, supplementary relatives and interpolations. They are not dependents and are set off by punctuation.
concepts.note: Supplementation is treated in Chapter 15 alongside coordination; the exact section is not cited because it falls outside the verified contents page. In the trees the supplement records its anchor.

concepts.name: The passive
concepts.orientation: In a passive clause the subject corresponds to the object of the active, the verb is be (or get) plus a past participle, and the agent is optional, in a by-phrase.
concepts.note: The by-phrase is labelled internalised complement: it expresses what would be the subject in the active. The passive is also discussed in Chapter 16; the exact section there falls outside the verified contents page.

concepts.name: Extraposition
concepts.orientation: A subordinate clause subject can be placed at the end, with dummy it in subject position: It is obvious that Kim lied.
concepts.note: The extraposed clause is labelled extraposed subject. Extraposition is an information-packaging construction: the version with the clause at the end is much more frequent.

concepts.name: Clause polarity
concepts.orientation: A clause as a whole is positive or negative, and simple tests tell which: a negative clause takes a positive tag (… is she?) and can be continued with neither. Negative meaning inside a word does not by itself make the clause negative.
concepts.note: The tests used here are the reversed-polarity tag (is she? after a negative clause, isn't she? after a positive one) and continuations with neither or not even (negative) versus so (positive). Affixal negation, as in unhappy, gives a negative meaning but a positive clause.

concepts.name: Verbal negation
concepts.orientation: In verbal negation the marker of negation goes with the verb: a negative auxiliary form such as didn't or isn't, or not after an auxiliary. A lexical verb needs the auxiliary do to be negated.
concepts.note: Negation of a finite clause through its verb is primary verbal negation; not before a non-finite verb, as in not to know, is secondary verbal negation. Not is treated in these trees as an adverb phrase in the VP of the auxiliary or non-finite clause; the analysis follows the catenative treatment of auxiliaries used elsewhere in this explorer.

concepts.name: Non-verbal negation
concepts.orientation: Negation can also be marked away from the verb: by not modifying a phrase, or by an absolute negator such as no, nobody, nothing or never. It may make the whole clause negative (clausal) or stay inside its phrase (subclausal).
concepts.note: Whether non-verbal negation is clausal is decided by the same polarity tests as for verbal negation: Kim found no errors takes the tag did she?, while Pat finished in no time takes didn't she?

concepts.name: Approximate negators
concepts.orientation: Few, little, rarely, seldom, hardly, scarcely and barely express a small amount rather than none, yet they pattern with negators: a clause containing one usually counts as negative by the tests.

concepts.name: Scope of negation
concepts.orientation: Negation has scope over part of a clause's meaning. An adjunct can fall inside the scope of the negation or outside it, and its position often shows which.
concepts.note: In these trees the difference in scope is matched by a difference in structure: an adjunct before the negative auxiliary is a dependent in the auxiliary's own VP, while one after it is inside the auxiliary's complement clause. Scope is a matter of meaning, so it is not always shown by structure like this.

concepts.name: Polarity-sensitive items
concepts.orientation: Some items are sensitive to polarity. Negatively-oriented ones (NPIs) such as any, ever and yet need a negative or other non-affirmative context; positively-oriented ones (PPIs) such as some and already resist negation.

concepts.name: Comparison of equality and inequality
concepts.orientation: A comparison states either a difference (inequality: taller than, less often than) or a sameness (equality: as tall as). This cuts across a second distinction, between scalar comparison of degrees and non-scalar comparison of identity or likeness.
concepts.note: The comparison in The delay was more annoying than serious is sometimes called metalinguistic: it compares how well two descriptions fit, so only more is used, even with adjectives that otherwise inflect.

concepts.name: Comparative complements and governors
concepts.orientation: A comparative complement such as than Pat or as Pat is licensed by a comparative governor: more, less, as, same, or a comparative inflection. Than and as are treated as prepositions heading the complement.
concepts.note: When the governor is a dependent rather than the head, as more is in more books than Pat, the complement is licensed indirectly. These trees attach such a complement to the phrase that contains both the governor and the head, labelled Complement with the construction named.

concepts.name: Comparative clauses
concepts.orientation: The complement of than or as is often a clause, and a reduced one: a comparative clause leaves out material understood from the main clause, always including the expression of the degree being compared.
concepts.note: The missing degree element is shown as a gap linked to the comparative phrase in the main clause. Whether than plus a single NP (than Pat) is itself a reduced clause is a question the trees here do not settle: they show the NP as the complement of than.

concepts.name: Analytic comparatives with more and less
concepts.orientation: Comparison of inequality is marked either inside the word (taller, tallest) or analytically, with more, most, less and least before an adjective or adverb. Which is used depends mainly on the length and shape of the base.
concepts.note: More and less are treated as determinatives, the comparative forms of much and little, functioning as modifiers in the AdjP or AdvP; this matches the treatment of much in much better elsewhere in the explorer.

concepts.name: Superlatives and set comparison
concepts.orientation: A superlative compares one member of a set with all the others (the oldest house in the street). With a set of only two, the comparative is the usual choice in careful usage (the younger of the two).

concepts.name: Non-scalar comparison
concepts.orientation: Some comparisons concern identity or likeness, not degree: the same as, similar to, different from, like. They have their own governors and complements, and no scale is involved.

concepts.name: Deixis
concepts.orientation: Deictic expressions are interpreted from the situation of utterance: who is speaking, to whom, where and when. I, you, here, this and that change their reference with every speaker and setting.
concepts.note: Here and there are treated as prepositions without a complement, as elsewhere in this explorer. Deictic and anaphoric are uses, not categories: there is anaphoric in the third example.

concepts.name: Anaphora and antecedents
concepts.orientation: An anaphor is an expression whose interpretation comes from another expression, its antecedent. Pronouns are the central anaphors, but the antecedent need not be an NP, and an anaphor need not be a pronoun.
concepts.note: Antecedent links are drawn only between expressions in the same example, and only on the reading described. They record interpretation, so they sit alongside the tree rather than in it.

concepts.name: Order of anaphor and antecedent
concepts.orientation: The antecedent usually comes first, but an anaphor can come before it (anticipatory anaphora), most freely when the anaphor is inside a subordinate construction that comes first.

concepts.name: Reflexive pronouns
concepts.orientation: Reflexive pronouns (myself, herself, themselves) have two uses: as complements, where they normally need a close antecedent such as the subject of their clause; and as emphatic additions to a clause.
concepts.note: The emphatic reflexive at the end of the clause is shown as an adjunct in the VP; its category is NP, like a reflexive object. Reciprocals (each other, one another) are related but not covered in this version.

concepts.name: Demonstratives
concepts.orientation: This, that, these and those are demonstrative determinatives. Their central use is deictic, contrasting near and far from the speaker; they also point back into the text or conversation (anaphoric use).

concepts.name: Pro-forms
concepts.orientation: Pro-forms stand in for expressions of many kinds, not only NPs: pro-nominal one replaces a nominal (a blue one), and so can replace a whole clause after verbs like think.
concepts.note: Pro-nominal one and the fused-head construction are alternatives: a blue one has one as head of the nominal, while the blue fuses the modifier with the head. Anaphoric so is treated here as an adverb functioning as complement.

concepts.name: Lexical bases and inflection
concepts.orientation: An inflected word-form is built from a lexical base by a morphological operation: usually adding a suffix (lamp, lamps), sometimes changing the base itself (goose, geese). The lexeme stays the same; only its form changes.
concepts.note: Word structures in this explorer are drawn as trees inside a single word: the word at the top, its bases and affixes below. The pieces are parts of a word, so they have categories such as Suffix but are not words themselves, and they are never selectable as phrases.

concepts.name: Spelling alternations
concepts.orientation: Adding a suffix can change how the base is written: a final consonant may double (stop, stopping), a silent e may drop (hope, hoping), and y may become i (carry, carries). The base is the same; only its written shape alternates.
concepts.note: Each base that changes its spelling records the plain base and the alternation, and the builder checks that the alternation really produces the written piece.

concepts.name: Inflectional grade
concepts.orientation: Adjectives and some adverbs inflect for grade: plain (big), comparative (bigger) and superlative (biggest). Short bases take the suffixes; longer ones mostly use more and most instead.

concepts.name: Plural formation
concepts.orientation: Most nouns form the plural with ·s, but some modify the base (knife, knives), some have a plural identical to the singular (sheep), and in some compounds the plural is marked inside (passers-by).

concepts.name: Regular and irregular verb forms
concepts.orientation: Regular verbs make the preterite and the past participle with ·ed. Irregular verbs use other operations: a change of vowel (eat, ate), a ·en past participle (eaten), or a mixture of the two.

concepts.name: Negative auxiliary forms
concepts.orientation: Auxiliary verbs have negative forms such as isn't, didn't and won't. These are inflected forms of the verb, not a verb plus a shortened not, which is why they behave as single words.

concepts.name: Morphological structure
concepts.orientation: Complex words have internal structure: bases, to which affixes attach (prefixes before, suffixes after), built up in layers. Unhappiness is un- plus happy first, then plus -ness, not un- plus happiness.

concepts.name: Derivational affixation
concepts.orientation: Derivation makes new lexemes by adding affixes: kind gives kindness (adjective to noun), modern gives modernise (adjective to verb). Unlike inflection, it can change the category and the meaning in less predictable ways.

concepts.name: Compounds
concepts.orientation: A compound combines two bases into one word: blackbird, bookshelf, well-known. It can mean something its parts do not predict, and it behaves as a single word, unlike a phrase of the same words.

concepts.name: Conversion
concepts.orientation: Conversion makes a word of a new category with no change of form: the noun bottle gives the verb bottle, the verb walk gives the noun walk. The new lexeme takes the inflections of its new category.

concepts.name: Clipping, blending and back-formation
concepts.orientation: Some words are made by shortening or merging rather than by adding affixes: clipping (laboratory to lab), blending (breakfast and lunch to brunch) and back-formation (editor to edit).

concepts.name: Primary terminals
concepts.orientation: A sentence written on its own ends with a primary terminal: a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. The choice signals the kind of speech act, and it need not match the clause type.
concepts.note: Punctuation marks are modelled separately from the constituent trees. Each mark is attached to a boundary of one constituent (its start, its end, or between two of its parts); the builder checks that the mark really sits at that boundary and that every punctuation mark in a punctuated example is accounted for.

concepts.name: Commas, semicolons and colons
concepts.orientation: The secondary boundary marks, comma, semicolon and colon, mark boundaries inside a sentence. Each one attaches to a boundary between constituents: the structure decides where a mark can go, and the mark helps the reader find the structure.

concepts.name: Delimiting commas, dashes and parentheses
concepts.orientation: Some marks set off a constituent on both sides: two commas, two dashes or a pair of parentheses around a supplement. When the supplement ends the sentence, the full stop takes the place of the closing comma or dash.

concepts.name: Quotation marks
concepts.orientation: Quotation marks set off words presented as someone else's, or as words in their own right. They delimit a constituent like a pair of brackets, but what they signal is the status of the words, not their grammar.

concepts.name: Hyphens and word-level punctuation
concepts.orientation: Word-level punctuation works inside words: a hyphen joins the parts of some compounds, and an apostrophe marks a genitive or a negative form. Unlike commas, these marks belong to words, not to boundaries between constituents.

confusions.label: Category vs function
confusions.orientation: Noun phrase names what it is; subject or object names its role.

confusions.label: Determinative vs determiner
confusions.orientation: A word class and a function in the NP, with different members.

confusions.label: Complement vs adjunct
confusions.orientation: The same PP can be either, depending on the verb.

confusions.label: Adjective vs adverb
confusions.orientation: Calm describes Kim; calmly describes the speaking.

confusions.label: Gerund vs participle
confusions.orientation: One verb form, distinct from nouns in -ing.

confusions.label: Relative vs interrogative
confusions.orientation: What Pat cooked: an NP after ate, a clause after asked.

confusions.label: Subject vs agent
confusions.orientation: A syntactic function versus a semantic role.

confusions.label: Predicative complement vs object
confusions.orientation: Both follow the verb; only one is a participant.

confusions.label: Coordination vs supplementation
confusions.orientation: Equal coordinates versus a loosely attached supplement.

confusions.label: Preposition vs subordinator
confusions.orientation: Because heads a PP; that only marks a clause.

confusions.label: Negative meaning vs negative clause
confusions.orientation: Unhappy is negative in meaning; the clause is still positive.

confusions.label: Than: preposition or conjunction?
confusions.orientation: Than heads a PP; its complement is an NP or a reduced clause.

confusions.label: Reflexive vs emphatic herself
confusions.orientation: An object that is required versus an optional addition.

confusions.label: Inflection vs derivation
confusions.orientation: A form of the same lexeme versus a new lexeme.

confusions.label: Compound vs phrase
confusions.orientation: Blackbird is one word; black bird is an NP.

confusions.label: Hyphen vs dash
confusions.orientation: A hyphen joins parts of a word; a dash sets off a supplement.
